title: A naming grammar for Netflix Tudum headlines, with Discord's blog as a control

slots.name: Title
slots.description: The franchise, film, or documentary's proper name. Sometimes stylized in small caps for effect (A HOUSE OF DYNAMITE), sometimes single-quoted ('Adolescence', 'Steve'), most often bare Title Case.

slots.name: Season / episode marker
slots.description: "Season N" or "Episode N", appended directly to TITLE. Optional; present on returning-series pages, absent on films, documentaries, and season-1 pages.

slots.name: Companion-content tag
slots.description: A fixed noun naming what KIND of companion page this is. Always sits immediately after TITLE (+ optional SEASON_EP) and immediately before a colon -- it is the hinge the whole headline turns on.

slots.name: Count
slots.description: A cardinal number, numeral or spelled out, observed from 3 to 41 in this corpus. Headline-initial in the dominant ordering; medial after a fronted CTA_VERB in the minority ordering (see count_listicle below).

slots.name: Superlative / attribute adjective
slots.description: Evaluative adjective modifying UNIT. Optional even inside count_listicle -- roughly half the listicle headlines skip it and go straight from COUNT to UNIT.

slots.name: Content-type unit noun
slots.description: The plural noun a COUNT counts. A small, closed, reused set.

slots.name: Connector verb phrase
slots.description: Infinitive or relative clause linking UNIT to a payoff for the reader.
example_fills: You Can Watch in a Weekend
to Take You on an Epic Journey
That Will Transport You Back to High School

slots.name: Temporal urgency tag
slots.description: Optional closer that manufactures a reason to click now.

slots.name: Colon clause
slots.description: Free clause after a colon that elaborates, promises, or asks. The one slot that carries no closed fill set anywhere in the corpus -- it is where the grammar hands control back to a human writer.
example_fills: Who's Who in the Twisty Thriller?
Get to Know the Family, Their Foes, and More

slots.name: Question frame
slots.description: Casts a clause (or the whole headline) as a WH- or yes/no question. Can BE the headline (question family) or fill just the COLON_CLAUSE half of another family (cast_guide, ending_explained).

slots.name: True-story marker
slots.description: A small closed set of frames for fact-checking a documentary or based-on-a-true-story claim -- exists only because Tudum publishes documentaries.
example_fills: Is [Title] Based on a True Story?
[Title] Is Based on a True Story of...

slots.name: Imperative CTA verb
slots.description: The imperative verb opening a headline. A closed, reused inventory -- most fills recur across many headlines rather than being coined fresh each time.

slots.name: Genre-pun verb
slots.description: A verb or verb phrase chosen because its literal sense puns on the specific title's own premise. Not a lookup from a fill list -- every instance is coined fresh from that one title's logline. See "the single most interesting rule" below.
example_fills: Chases Down No. 1 (I Will Find You)
Journeys to No. 1 (Little House on the Prairie)

slots.name: Weekly-rank status
slots.description: Fixed collocation closing a top10_ranking headline. Exactly two forms observed.
example_fills: at No. 1 for a Second Week

slots.name: Award event name
slots.description: Proper noun of an awards ceremony.

slots.name: From/to franchise pair
slots.description: Two TITLE slots joined by "From ... to ...", always closing on the fixed tag "What to Watch on Netflix". The most rigid creative-content family in the corpus -- only the two title fills vary, week to week.
example_fills: From The Hawk to Shipwrecked: Nightmare at Sea

tudum.name: Count listicle
example_headlines: 28 Gripping True Crime Documentaries to Stream
6 Movies Starring Best Buds and The Rip Stars Ben Affleck and Matt Damon
The 22 Scariest Things to Watch Right Now
41 Comedies to Watch Whenever You Need a Laugh
12 Documentaries to Stream About Cults and Cult-Like Figures
11 Gripping Detective Shows to Solve the Mystery of Your Next Stream
constraints: COUNT is headline-initial in the dominant ordering (15 of 18) -- "28 Gripping True Crime Documentaries to Stream".

In the minority ordering (3 of 18) COUNT is fronted instead by a CTA_VERB + "These": "Download These 12 Movies and Series Before Your Next Flight" -- COUNT never appears mid-headline without either the sentence-initial position or a "These" pivot in front of it.
SUPERLATIVE is skipped in slightly under half of instances -- the frame tolerates a bare COUNT + UNIT ("41 Comedies to Watch...").
UNIT never co-occurs with CONTENT_TYPE_TAG -- no listicle headline in the corpus also carries a "Cast:" or "Trailer:" tag.

generated_novel.text: 16 Underrated Neo-Noir Thrillers to Watch This Winter
generated_novel.why: Every slot fill is drawn from an attested class (COUNT in range, SUPERLATIVE adjective, UNIT noun, seasonal TEMPORAL_URGENCY) and the ordering matches the dominant pattern.

generated_novel.text: Amber Hollow and 9 Other Slow-Burn Mysteries for a Rainy Weekend
generated_novel.why: Opens with a TITLE ahead of the count, which the real corpus never does for this family -- but it reads fine because it borrows the ordering from count_listicle_inline (COUNT is still fronted by a pivot phrase, just "and N Other" instead of "These N"). Flagged as an extrapolation beyond the attested pivot set, not a violation of it.

generated_novel.text: Comedies
generated_novel.why: COUNT and CONNECTOR_VP are both obligatory in every attested instance; dropping them doesn't produce a degenerate but still-plausible headline, it produces a category label. The grammar has no optional path that reduces this far.

tudum.name: Title-clause apposition
example_headlines: 13 Going on 30 : Emily Bader and Logan Lerman Star in the Rom-Com Reboot
A Toxic Love Story Documentary: Who Is Lilithistruth? Where Is Michelle Hadley Now? Angela and Ian Jail Update
Adolescence Episode 3: Inside the ‘Chess Match’ Between Jamie and Briony
Adolescence : Stephen Graham Explains the ‘Poetry’ of That Final Scene
How the Avatar: The Last Airbender Season 2 Finale Sets Up Season 3
From Coney Island to Water Street: Black Rabbit 's NYC Filming Tour
constraints: The most generic and most productive family -- COLON_CLAUSE is unconstrained free text, so this is the fallback pattern for any headline that wants to name a subject and then say something about it without picking a more specific CONTENT_TYPE_TAG.

Overlaps in SURFACE FORM with cast_guide / trailer / ending_explained / everything_to_know / true_story / from_x_to_y_watch, which is why it is checked last among the colon-bearing rules -- it only claims headlines none of the more specific tags claimed first.

generated_novel.text: The Undertow Season 2: A Heist Crew Splinters Under New Leadership
generated_novel.why: TITLE + SEASON_EP + free COLON_CLAUSE is exactly the attested shape.

generated_novel.text: Paper Wasps: What the Season 1 Finale Sets Up for Season 2

tudum.notes: Because COLON_CLAUSE is an open slot, this family is a poor test of the grammar's precision on its own -- its coverage number mostly reflects how often Tudum uses a colon at all, not a specific creative choice.

tudum.name: Imperative CTA opener
example_headlines: Enter A HOUSE OF DYNAMITE, Kathryn Bigelow’s New Thriller
Watch Aria Mia Loberti and Nell Sutton’s ‘All the Light We Cannot See’ Auditions
Go Inside the Uplifting Ending of All the Light We Cannot See
Prepare to Be Swept Away By ‘All the Light We Cannot See’
Watch These Cillian Murphy Movies and Series — By Order of the Peaky Blinders
Say Ciao from Emily in Paris Season 4’s French and Italian Filming Locations
constraints: CTA_VERB is drawn from a closed, reused list (~16 attested forms); it is not coined fresh per headline the way GENRE_PUN_VERB is.

This slot's opener position is mutually exclusive with CONTENT_TYPE_TAG -- zero headlines in the corpus both open with a CTA_VERB and also carry a Cast:/Trailer:/Ending Explained: tag. A headline picks one organizing device, not both.

"Meet" is common enough (4 of 20) and specifically tied to introducing a cast that it is worth naming as its own sub-rule: Meet + [the] + TITLE (+ possessive) + Cast + COLON_CLAUSE, effectively an imperative-fronted variant of cast_guide.

generated_novel.text: Go Undercover with the Half Moon Bay Investigators
Meet the Redshift Cast Charting a Course Out of the Blackout
Enter the Cobalt County Sheriff's Department
generated_novel.why: Grammatically fine, but "Enter" is attested exactly once in the corpus ("Enter A HOUSE OF DYNAMITE"), paired with a stylized all-caps title for a specific prestige-thriller launch. Reusing it on an ordinary Title Case procedural show borrows a CTA_VERB fill without the register it was attested with -- a reminder that a closed fill list is not the same as a fill list with no register constraints.

tudum.name: Ending explained
example_headlines: 'Adolescence' Episode 4 Recap: Creators and Star Explain Ending and Why Jamie Killed Katie
Avatar: The Last Airbender Ending Explained: Inside the Fiery Finale
Enola Holmes 3 Ending Explained: What Happens to Enola and Tewkesbury?
I Will Find You Ending Explained: What Happened to Matthew?
Little House on the Prairie Ending Explained: What’s Next for the Ingalls Family
The Man on Fire Ending, Explained: Yahya Abdul-Mateen II Breaks It Down
constraints: COLON_CLAUSE after the tag is a question in the majority of instances ("What Happens to Enola and Tewkesbury?", "Did Valeria Find Her Children?") but not always ("Inside the Fiery Finale").
This family and true_story are the two places QUESTION_FRAME most often lives INSIDE another family's COLON_CLAUSE rather than governing the whole headline.

generated_novel.text: The Undertow Ending Explained: Did the Money Ever Actually Exist?
Amber Hollow Season 2 Ending, Explained: What Happens to the Sheriff?

tudum.name: Awards coverage
example_headlines: The 2026 Actor Awards Presented by SAG-AFTRA: See the Full List of Winners
Frankenstein Leads Netflix Films in 2026 BAFTA Nominations
KPop Demon Hunters and Frankenstein Shine at the 2026 BAFTA Film Awards
Inside the 2026 BAFTA TV Awards Celebration
From Adolescence to Nobody Wants This: A Toast to Netflix’s 2025 Emmy Nominees
Adolescence Grows Into an Emmy Winner, Nabbing 8 Trophies at the 2025 Emmy Awards
constraints: The verb here is often celebratory rather than genre-punning ("Leads", "Shine", "Reunite", "Honors") -- a softer, less content-aware cousin of the GENRE_PUN_VERB device seen in top10_ranking.

AWARD_EVENT is a genuinely closed set in this corpus: every instance names one of BAFTA, the Emmys, the Oscars, the Grammys, SAG-AFTRA/the Actor Awards, or a Fellowship gala -- no other award body appears.

generated_novel.text: Amber Hollow Leads the Field in 2027 Emmy Nominations
The Undertow Cast Reunites at the Golden Globes
generated_novel.why: The Golden Globes never appears in the attested AWARD_EVENT set. This is exactly the failure mode a closed-set slot is supposed to catch: the sentence is fluent English but reaches outside the fill set this specific brand's coverage actually uses (worth checking against a longer corpus before trusting the exclusion, but it is a real gap at this sample size).

tudum.name: Rhetorical question

template.note: governs the whole headline, WH- or yes/no

example_headlines: America’s Sweethearts Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders: Why Did Reece Retire?
Where Was Season 2 of The Four Seasons Filmed?
Little House on the Prairie Surprise Cameo: Did You Spot Alison Arngrim?
Which Couples Are Still Together from Every Season of Love Is Blind ?
Have You Watched All of Netflix’s Top 10 Most Popular Movies?
Who Wins Perfect Match Season 4 And Which Couples Are Still Together?
constraints: Distinct from true_story's QUESTION_FRAME use in that these questions are about plot/status/cast ("Where Was It Filmed?", "Does X Return?"), never about factual veracity -- that specific question shape is reserved for true_story.

generated_novel.text: Is the Redshift Crew Getting a Season 3?
Where Was Amber Hollow Filmed?

tudum.name: Trailer drop

template.note: an alternative realization fronts a CTA_VERB instead of the tag: "Watch the Trailer for..."

example_headlines: Enola Holmes 3 Trailer: Millie Bobby Brown Chases After a Kidnapped Sherlock
I Will Find You Trailer: Sam Worthington Hunts for the Truth
The Little House on the Prairie Trailer Expands Laura Ingalls’s World
Watch the Trailer for My Life with the Walter Boys Season 3
Office Romance Trailer: Love Takes Flight in This New Jennifer Lopez Movie
The Ransom Canyon Season 2 Trailer Welcomes Minka Kelly and Josh Duhamel Home
constraints: Two competing realizations of the same content-type event: TITLE-first with a trailing "Trailer:" tag (majority), or CTA_VERB-first ("Watch/Buckle Up and Watch the Trailer for...") -- the only family where the CTA_VERB-opener and CONTENT_TYPE_TAG strategies are NOT mutually exclusive, because the tag "Trailer" is doing double duty as both the content-type marker and the object of the CTA verb.

generated_novel.text: The Undertow Trailer: A Crew Splits Over One Bag of Money
Buckle Up and Watch the Trailer for Amber Hollow

tudum.name: True-story fact-check
example_headlines: Is Apple Cider Vinegar a True Story? Creator Explains Belle Gibson Inspiration, Ending
Enola Holmes 3: Learn the True Story Behind the Film
Is l Will Find You Based on a True Story? All About the Harlan Coben Novel and Series Adaptation
The True Story of Maternal Instinct Documentary’s Terrifying Pregnancy Secret
Shipwrecked Nightmare at Sea Documentary: Costa Concordia True Story, Francesco Schettino, Status Update
Should I Marry a Murderer? : The True Story of Caroline Muirhead
constraints: Exists only because Tudum covers documentaries and based-on-a-true-story dramas -- a content-domain constraint, not a purely formal one.

TRUE_STORY_MARKER has exactly four attested surface realizations in this corpus (see the slot inventory); a fifth invented shape (e.g. "Fact or Fiction: X") would be a plausible-sounding EXTRAPOLATION, not an attested fill.

generated_novel.text: Is The Quiet Part Based on a True Story?
The True Story Behind Amber Hollow's Vanishing Sheriff

tudum.name: Cast guide

template.fixed: Cast / Cast Guide / Cast and Characters

example_headlines: Enola Holmes 3 Cast and Characters: Get Reacquainted with Your Favorite Sleuths
House of Guinness Cast: Get to Know the Family, Their Foes, and More
I Will Find You Cast : Who’s Who in the Twisty Thriller?
ONE PIECE Season 2 Cast: Meet the Live-Action New and Returning Characters
Ransom Canyon Season 2 Cast: Who’s Back in Texas — and Who’s New in Town?
Meet the Running Point Cast: Kate Hudson Leads the Starting Lineup
constraints: COLON_CLAUSE after "Cast:" is almost always an imperative ("Get to Know...", "Meet the...") or a question ("Who's Who...?") -- a free clause in principle, but in practice drawing from the same small set of moves as imperative_opener and question.

generated_novel.text: The Undertow Cast Guide: Meet the Crew Behind the Job

tudum.name: Weekly Top 10 ranking

template.note: an optional punny lead-in before the title, e.g. "Adventure Is Afoot:"

example_headlines: The Rip Confiscates the No. 1 Spot in This Week’s Top 10
The Rip Is Right on the Money at No. 1 in This Week’s Top 10
Little House on the Prairie Journeys to No. 1 in This Week’s Top 10
Enola Holmes Cracks the Case, Holding No. 1 in This Week’s Top 10
I Will Find You Chases Down No. 1 in This Week’s Top 10
Adventure Is Afoot: Enola Holmes 3 Takes No. 1 in This Week’s Top 10
constraints: GENRE_PUN_VERB is obligatory and is never reused across two different titles in this corpus -- every single instance is bespoke to that week's show. This is the family "the single most interesting rule" below is drawn from.

RANK_STATUS has exactly two forms: "in This Week's Top 10" for a title's first appearance at No. 1, "for a Second Week" (etc.) once it repeats -- an ordering/state constraint (you cannot get the second-week form without a first-week instance existing in the same series of posts, though that history is outside any single headline).

generated_novel.text: The Undertow Makes Off With No. 1 in This Week's Top 10
generated_novel.why: "Makes off with" puns on the show's heist premise, matching the attested device exactly.

generated_novel.text: Amber Hollow Takes No. 1 in This Week's Top 10
generated_novel.why: Grammatical and frame-correct, but "Takes" is a generic verb with no relationship to what Amber Hollow is about -- exactly the kind of fill this family's real examples never use. It shows the grammar's most content-aware rule is easy to satisfy FORMALLY while missing it substantively; a generator that only checks the frame, not the pun, will produce headlines that are wrong in the way this family is never wrong in the real corpus.

tudum.name: From/to recirculation digest
example_headlines: From The Hawk to Shipwrecked: Nightmare at Sea : What to Watch on Netflix
From WWE: Unreal to Heartstopper Forever : What to Watch on Netflix
From 72 Hours to Hannibal : What to Watch on Netflix
From Little House on the Prairie to Dark Winds : What to Watch on Netflix
From I Will Find You to Maternal Instinct : What to Watch on Netflix
From Color Book to The American Experiment : What to Watch on Netflix
constraints: The most rigid family in the corpus: 8 of 8 instances share the identical frame with only the two TITLE fills changing. A weekly digest post, not a one-off editorial choice.

generated_novel.text: From The Undertow to Amber Hollow: What to Watch on Netflix

tudum.name: Now-streaming announcement
example_headlines: Bridgerton Season 4 Is Now Streaming: See Benedict and Sophie’s Romance Heat Up
Kevin Hart’s Wild 72 Hours Is Now Streaming
Little Brother Is Streaming: John Cena and Eric André Are Family in New Movie
New on Netflix in July 2026
Saddle Up: Season 2 of Ransom Canyon Is Now Streaming
Season 2 of The Four Seasons Is Now Streaming: Take Another Trip Around the Sun
constraints: "New on Netflix in [Month Year]" is a distinct, calendar-anchored realization of the same PLATFORM_CTA idea rather than a TITLE-anchored one -- the only instance in this family where TITLE is absent entirely.

generated_novel.text: The Undertow Is Now Streaming: A Crew Splits Over One Bag of Money

tudum.name: Everything-to-know explainer

template.fixed: Everything You Need to Know / Everything to Know About...

example_headlines: 3 Body Problem: Everything You Need to Know About the Series
Adolescence : Everything to Know About the Emmy-Winning One-Shot Crime Drama
Love on the Spectrum Season 5: Everything You Need to Know
Everything to Know about the Mexican Thriller No One Saw Us Leave
The Ultimatum: Marry or Move On Season 4: Everything You Need to Know
constraints: Functions as a catch-all promise of comprehensiveness -- used on news-hub pages that don't fit a more specific tag (Cast/Trailer/Ending).

generated_novel.text: Amber Hollow Season 2: Everything You Need to Know

discord_blog.name: Patch notes / changelog
example_headlines: Discord Patch Notes: April 2024
Discord Patch Notes: April 3, 2025
Discord Patch Notes: April 6, 2026
Discord Patch Notes: August 1, 2024
Discord Patch Notes: August 30, 2024
Discord Patch Notes: August 4, 2025
discord_blog.notes: Zero editorial content -- the only variable is a date. The single most rigid family in EITHER corpus, and it has no Tudum equivalent because Tudum has no engineering/release surface to log. This is closer to a database record with a naming convention than a headline in the entertainment-editorial sense.

discord_blog.name: Title-clause apposition
example_headlines: Access: A New Portal for Managing Internal Authorization
Attention Server Owners: The App Directory is Here!
Authenticity Matters: Discord's Pride Month 2025
Avatar Decorations & Profile Effects: Collect and Keep the Newest Styles
You’ve Got (Too Much) Mail: Behind the Scenes of the 3/25/26 Voice Outage
Building on the Social Layer of Games: What’s New from GDC 2026
discord_blog.notes: Same shape as Tudum's colon_subtitle and proportionally even more common here (18.3% vs 12.5%) -- this looks like a genuinely brand-independent editorial default rather than something either brand invented.

discord_blog.name: Imperative CTA opener
example_headlines: Queue Up Your Playlists on Discord with the Amazon Music Listening Party Activity!
Celebrate Arcane’s Second Season with a new Shop Collection
Come Build Where the World Plays
Celebrate Discord’s 8th Birthday with Free Activities and More
Celebrate Discord’s 11th Birthday with an Exclusive Set of Emoji and Wallpapers
Protecting Against Scams on Discord
discord_blog.notes: The CTA_VERB fill set overlaps with Tudum's (Watch, Check Out, Celebrate, Buckle Up-adjacent forms) but Discord adds its own: Queue Up, Ready Your, Save and, Set Out, Welcome, Come Build, Introducing. Shared DEVICE, brand-specific vocabulary.

discord_blog.name: How-to instructional
example_headlines: How to Make and Use Custom Emoji on Discord
How to Use Nitro: A Beginner’s Guide to Discord’s Premium Subscription
How to Change Your Theme to Bring Your Vibe to Discord
How to Create & Upload Your Own Stickers on Discord
How to Customize Your Discord Profile
How to Link Discord to Battlefield 6, Marvel Rivals & More
discord_blog.notes: No equivalent family exists anywhere in the Tudum sample -- Tudum has nothing to instruct a reader how to DO, only things to watch. A content-domain difference surfacing directly as a naming-grammar difference.

discord_blog.name: Engineering deep-dive
example_headlines: How We’re Building the Future of Discord
How Discord Automates ScyllaDB Clusters at Scale

discord_blog.name: Staff picks roundup
example_headlines: December Staff Picks: It’s Giving Games
June's Staff Picks: Summertime Game Time
Staff Picks, April 2025: All The Adaptations
Staff Picks, June 2025: Summer of Showcases
Staff Picks, May 2025: The Games That Brought Us to Discord
Staff Picks, September 2025: Welcome to Our Video Game Museum
discord_blog.notes: Discord's rough structural cousin of Tudum's from_x_to_y_watch digest family -- a recurring curated-roundup slot -- but keyed to a MONTH rather than to two franchise names, because Discord's roundup curates external games, not its own catalog.

discord_blog.name: All-caps shout
example_headlines: MULTIPLAYER SEQUEL TO ACCLAIMED AAAA GAME “THE LAST MEADOW” ANNOUNCED: PLAYABLE NOW
WHO LIVES ON YOUR PROFILE FOR ALL TO SEE? 🎶 SPONGEBOB, IN THE SHOP!
*FLAILS AROUND* SUMMER SPECIAL! JOIN NITRO, GET AN EXTRA MONTH OF NITRO ON US!
MAJOR NEWS: DISCORD ANNOUNCES ITS FIRST IN-HOUSE AAAA VIDEO GAME, “THE LAST MEADOW”
discord_blog.notes: Zero instances anywhere in the 240-headline Tudum sample. A real, clean, register-level brand difference: Discord's shop/promo copy permits shouting, emoji, and stage-direction asterisks (*FLAILS AROUND*); Tudum's voice holds sentence case even in its most hype-driven weekly content (Top 10 rankings, awards coverage).

discord_blog.name: Meet-imperative
example_headlines: Meet DAVE: Discord’s New End-to-End Encryption for Audio & Video
discord_blog.notes: Present in both corpora (Tudum 4, Discord 1) at low volume -- a generic editorial device, not brand-specific, just used far more on Tudum because it has far more casts to introduce.

How Shawn Levy Crafted the Epic, Emotional ‘All the Light We Cannot See’ Series

tudum.commentary: The residue is not random -- it clusters almost entirely around one-off news and feature journalism: a set visit, an interview, an award-season reaction piece, a renewal announcement, a single magazine cover story. Those are ordinary declarative English sentences (Subject + vivid verb + Object) with an effectively unbounded verb vocabulary ("Cracks Open", "Carried His Baggage into", "Embraces Truthfulness in", "Grace the Covers of") -- there is no small fill set behind them the way there is behind Cast:/Trailer:/Ending Explained:. The grammar's coverage tracks a real editorial-production distinction: TEMPLATED hub content (list pages, cast pages, ending-explained pages, trailer pages, weekly Top 10 posts, the from/to digest) is close to fully formulaic; one-off NEWS content about a specific event is hand-written and resists slotting, on purpose -- a news headline that read like a template would undersell the news. That distinction is recoverable purely from surface headline form, without ever seeing Tudum's own internal content taxonomy.

sample: A Cornucopia of Updates Make Discord on Desktop Fresher Than a Crisp Fall Breeze
Discord is Your Place for AI with Friends
An Update on our Mental Health & Belonging Work
Announcing Discord’s Social SDK, Helping Power Your Game’s Social Experiences
Announcing Discord’s Social SDK, Helping Power Your Game’s Social Experiences
Discord Announces First Mobile Ad Format, Broadening Advertising Opportunities

Cost Attribution in Discord’s API
discord_blog.commentary: Discord's residue is more heterogeneous than Tudum's because Discord's blog spans more genres to begin with -- product announcements, community-partnership stories, executive-hire news, one-off promo copy, and reflective essays ("Passing the Torch", "Thank You for Ten Years") that read as personal rather than templated. Some of it IS a family that exists at too low a volume in this 200-page sample to justify a named row on its own (a handful of "Introducing X" openers were folded into imperative_opener; a handful of birthday/anniversary posts share a shape but number three). The honest read is that Discord's blog has a wider genre mix and a flatter distribution across it than Tudum's, which concentrates most of its volume into a smaller number of very-high-frequency evergreen hub types.

cooccurrence_rules: A headline picks exactly ONE organizing strategy from {CTA_VERB opener, CONTENT_TYPE_TAG colon frame, COUNT listicle opener, QUESTION_FRAME} and does not mix them -- the sole attested exception is the trailer family, where the tag "Trailer" itself can double as the CTA_VERB's object ("Watch the Trailer for...").
CONTENT_TYPE_TAG is always immediately preceded by TITLE (+ optional SEASON_EP) and never by COUNT, CTA_VERB, or a question word.
COUNT and CONTENT_TYPE_TAG never co-occur -- no listicle headline in the corpus also carries a Cast:/Trailer:/Ending Explained: tag.
GENRE_PUN_VERB is attested only paired with RANK_STATUS (the Top 10 family) -- it is the mechanism that keeps a near-fully-fixed weekly frame from reading as repetitive across dozens of instances.

SEASON_EP co-occurs with CONTENT_TYPE_TAG far more often than it appears alone -- most season/episode mentions exist specifically to scope a Cast/Trailer/Ending-Explained page to one season, not to open a headline on their own.

QUESTION_FRAME is mutually exclusive with a CONTENT_TYPE_TAG-initial reading of the WHOLE headline, but freely fills the COLON_CLAUSE half of a CONTENT_TYPE_TAG headline -- e.g. "I Will Find You Cast: Who's Who in the Twisty Thriller?" is CONTENT_TYPE_TAG-governed with a QUESTION_FRAME riding inside its COLON_CLAUSE.
TRUE_STORY_MARKER only appears on documentary or based-on-a-true-story titles -- a content-domain gate on a formal slot, not a purely syntactic one.

seo_title_layer.commentary: Every page carries two separately authored headline strings: the on-page <h1> (the corpus this whole schema is built from) and the <title> tag (what shows up in a search result or a browser tab). On Tudum these diverge in wording on 97.3% of pages -- not just different casing, genuinely different SENTENCES for the same article, drawn from a visibly different grammar: the <title> tag runs on a closed facet vocabulary (Cast, Trailer, Release Date, Plot, Photos, Ending, News...) strung together with commas after a colon, closer to a metadata record than a written sentence, while the <h1> is the narrative-sentence grammar documented above. On Discord's blog the two strings match on 100.0% of pages (187 of 187 valid h1-bearing pages, after excluding the 3 collection-artifact pages above) -- Discord authors one headline and reuses it verbatim in both places, almost without exception. That gap is itself a naming-grammar finding: Tudum runs two independently generated title systems for the same content (a machine-facing search-facet schema and a human-facing editorial sentence), Discord runs one.

most_interesting_rule.title: The weekly Top 10 headline's verb is picked to pun on what the show is ABOUT, not drawn from a list
most_interesting_rule.body: Every other slot in this grammar reduces to a fill set you could hand an agent as a closed vocabulary -- CONTENT_TYPE_TAG is 8 words, UNIT is 10 words, CTA_VERB is a list of 16 recurring imperatives. GENRE_PUN_VERB is the one slot that does not: in all 8 top10_ranking headlines, the verb phrase is coined fresh, and every single one is a pun on that specific show's own premise. A detective story "Cracks the Case." A heist thriller about stolen money "Confiscates the No. 1 Spot" and "Is Right on the Money." A missing-persons search thriller "Chases Down No. 1" and "Holds at No. 1." A frontier-travel family drama "Journeys to No. 1." A workplace romance "Enamors Viewers." A movie about shapeshifting critters has "The Critters of Swapped Soar to No. 1." The same device, at lower intensity, shows up in the awards_coverage and residue "talent spotlight" headlines (Louis Partridge "Cracks Open" House of Guinness). This is a rule about a PROCESS a human writer runs, not a lookup: to fill this slot correctly you have to know the show's logline, not just have a list of Top-10-appropriate verbs. It is also the clearest place the grammar breaks as a pure generation instrument -- see the top10_ranking family's "wrong" generated example above, where a grammatically perfect fill ("Takes No. 1") is exactly the kind of generic verb this family's real examples never use. A productive schema for this slot would need to take a one-line synopsis as an input, not just emit from a word list -- which is a genuinely different (and harder) kind of rule than every other slot in this corpus.

shared_rules.reading: Present at real volume on both, proportionally MORE common on Discord. Reads as a brand-independent default of editorial headline writing, not something either brand invented.

shared_rules.rule: Imperative CTA opener, incl. Meet- (imperative_opener + meet_imperative)
shared_rules.reading: Same device on both at close to the same volume, overlapping CTA_VERB fills (Watch, Check Out, Celebrate, Buckle-Up-adjacent forms), each brand adding its own extensions. "Meet" specifically (introducing a cast) is generic, not brand-specific -- Tudum simply has far more casts to introduce (4 of its 20 vs. 1 of Discord's 20).

The one shared rule proven by ABSENCE rather than presence: Tudum's voice holds sentence case everywhere in this sample, including its most hype-driven weekly content; Discord explicitly permits shouting registers in shop/promo copy. Both are real, brand-held choices, not accidents -- one just happens to be a floor, not a ceiling.

netflix_specific_rules: count_listicle (7.5% of Tudum, ~0% of Discord) -- true numbered listicles are a content-hub convention with no Discord-blog equivalent.
CONTENT_TYPE_TAG closed vocabulary (Cast/Trailer/Ending Explained/Recap) -- Discord's colon_subtitle clauses are freely composed, never drawn from a fixed content-type tag set.
true_story fact-checking frame -- exists only because Tudum covers documentaries.
top10_ranking + GENRE_PUN_VERB -- a weekly chart mechanism that only makes sense for a streaming catalog with its own real-time popularity ranking.
from_x_to_y_watch recirculation digest -- a fixed weekly template, absent from Discord.
now_streaming / awards_coverage -- content-calendar and awards-season coverage, both intrinsic to being a studio/publisher.
The <title>-vs-<h1> divergence itself (97.3% vs 0.0%) -- Netflix appears to run two independently generated headline systems per page; Discord runs one.
discord_specific_rules: patch_notes_changelog (25.9% of Discord, 0% of Tudum) -- a release-log naming convention with zero editorial slot variation, the most rigid family in either corpus, existing only because Discord has an engineering/release surface to log.
how_to + how_engineering (14.2% combined) -- instructional and technical-deep-dive registers, absent from Tudum's entertainment-only remit.

staff_picks -- a recurring curated-roundup naming convention keyed to a month, Discord's structural cousin of Tudum's from_x_to_y_watch but serving a different content domain (external games, not Discord's own catalog).
all_caps_shout -- a shouting register (full caps, emoji, exclamation, stage-direction asterisks) permitted in shop/promo copy, never observed on Tudum.
control_comparison.verdict: The control comparison does what it's supposed to: it separates the rules that are just how editorial headline writing works (colon apposition, imperative openers, a generic Meet-the-cast device) from the rules that are specifically Netflix's, because they only make sense for a company that runs a streaming catalog with weekly popularity charts, a documentary slate, and a content calendar -- and from the rules that are specifically Discord's, because they only make sense for a company that ships software and logs its own changes. Neither corpus's grammar transfers wholesale to the other; about a third of the fixed vocabulary each does have (CONTENT_TYPE_TAG, patch-notes date-stamping, the true-story marker) is legibly a function of what the two companies actually publish, not of house style in the abstract.

method.classification: Each headline was matched against an ordered list of regular-expression rules, first match wins, derived by close reading of the full raw headline dump for each corpus (see scripts/classify.py). A headline with no match is residue.
method.reproducibility: python3 scripts/extract_corpus.py && python3 scripts/classify.py && python3 scripts/build_grammar.py regenerates corpus.json, scripts/classified.json, and this file from the source page snapshots.
method.shelf_title_exclusion: Netflix's actual in-product shelf titles (row titles like "Trending Now" or a personalized row name) are personalized and sit behind authentication. They were not accessed, scraped, or otherwise obtained for this analysis -- this schema is derived entirely from public Tudum editorial headlines, which do the same classify/entice/set-expectation job a shelf title does but are publicly readable without a login.
